loss.why: What a wrong setup costs a lap (plan 5.2). Each parameter is worth its own seconds at full deviation and the nine together add to 1.85 s: a car nobody has dialled in is seconds off, which is what makes practice worth its hour. The wings and the floor matter most; the three sliders of the fine level are worth 0.6 s between them, which is why owning that level is worth the tenth or so the plan asks for — not because they are more important, but because a team that cannot touch them carries whatever the preset got wrong. Deviation is measured in points of the 0..100 scale: 18 points off is the full cost, and the quadratic with a 15% plateau means the couple of points either side of the optimum are free — the window matters, its exact centre does not.

ideal.why: Where the optimum moves with the conditions (plan 5.2: the ideal setup shifts with air and track temperature, wind and rain). The factory preset of the pack is the optimum at 35 °C of track, 15 km/h of wind and a dry surface; from there every degree hotter takes a quarter of a point off camber and a fifth off toe (a hot track overheats the tyre surface, so teams stop asking so much of it) and a tenth off each wing, while the car is lifted a tenth of a point to protect the floor. Wind is worth a tenth of a point of front wing and 0.15 of rear per km/h over the reference: a gusty track is won with stability, not with peak downforce. The preset itself is only decent, and how decent depends on the slider: the wings and the brakes are the same every year and the preset is 4 points off, the mechanical settings 6, and the fine three — camber, toe, gear ratios — 11, because those depend on this car and not on this track. The offset is drawn once per track per career, so a track is always wrong in the same direction, and a team that cannot touch the fine sliders carries that error all weekend: about a tenth of a second, which is what owning the third level is worth (plan 5.2). Rain moves everything at once — 8 to 10 points more wing, the car 7 points higher, the suspension 9 points softer, brake bias 6 points rearwards so the fronts do not lock — which is why a wet weekend makes Friday's numbers worthless.

access.why: Who may touch what (plan 5.2, fixed in the plan's own table). Mechanical setup — ride heights and stiffness — opens with a race engineer at 60 or a level-2 simulator: either road is open to any team that decides to walk it. The fine level — camber, toe, gear ratios — needs a race engineer at 78 and a level-3 simulator and a driver who can describe what the car does (feedback 65): three conditions at once, because that level is the privilege of a mature team. The thresholds are read per car, from that car's engineer and that car's driver, so team-mates can have different levels — and they do.

reading.why: How well the engineer can say where the optimum is (plan 5.2: the recommendation is a range, and its width comes from the engineer, the simulator, the driver's feedback and the laps already run here). A car that arrives without having run is set up on that reading alone, so this is also what a weekend without practice costs: 13.5 points of reading error is about half a second a lap through the loss curve — the 0.5 s a car off the truck was worth in M5. The people move it by a few points either way (a race engineer at 70 is the reference, each point worth 0.05, a simulator level 0.8, a point of driver feedback 0.02), so a strong crew turns up at 9 points and a weak one at 14: worth a quarter of a second between them before anybody drives. Setup laps close the rest on a 6-lap scale — six laps of setup work take the reading to 8 points and half an hour of it to 4.5, which is inside the plateau where the loss is zero. That is the trade of plan 5.3: an hour of running is worth more than any amount of staff.

feedback.why: What the driver says after a run (plan 5.2: the words point at a direction, never at a number). A parameter has to be at least 6 points out before it shows in the car at all — under that the driver has nothing to report. A driver with feedback at 60 blames the wrong thing three times in ten ("no front end" when the rear ride height is the problem); every point above takes 0.6% off that, down to a floor of 5%, because even the best driver describes a symptom and not a cause.
